bicycle.explore.title: How it works
captions: One turn of the pedals can carry a bike over six metres. Gears decide how far.
Pedals turn a big front chainring; the chain carries its turning to a small rear cog.
48 teeth in front, 16 behind: the rear wheel turns three times per pedal turn.
The price: the wheel turns faster, but the tyre pushes the road far more gently.
Each wheel turn rolls about 2.1 metres, so one pedal turn moves you 6.3 metres.
At 80 pedal turns a minute, that is 30 kilometres an hour.

bicycle.motion.title: Gear ratio
captions: The chain links a big front gear to a small rear gear, so one pedal turn spins the wheel more than once.
Gear ratio is front teeth divided by rear teeth. Each pedal turn pulls that many teeth of chain past the rear gear.
Energy is conserved: a higher ratio gives more speed per pedal turn but less push at the wheel.

bicycle.whatif.title: What if
captions: Fewer teeth at the back give more speed for the same pedalling: 44 km/h on the smallest gear, 14 on the largest.
The small front ring lowers every gear by about 30 percent. You go slower, but each push on the pedal is stronger.

bicycle.flow.title: Follow the force
captions: Your leg pushes the pedal down. The crank is a lever that turns the push into a twist on the front gear.
The front gear pulls the top of the chain tight. A clean chain loses only about 3 percent to friction.
The chain turns the rear gear. A small rear gear spins the wheel several times for every pedal turn.
The tyre pushes back on the road and the road pushes the bike forward. That push is what moves you.

bicycle.number.title: The number
captions: The front gear has three times the teeth of the rear, so the wheel turns three times per pedal turn: 6.3 metres.
At 80 pedal turns a minute that is 30 km/h. The price: the tyre pushes with only 17 percent of your pedal force.
A low gear swaps it round. Three times the push for climbing, but only 2.1 metres per turn.
